comments.author: @anncollings2573
comments.text:
This commentary is very wrong. I know a lot about of the island as I spent many hours studying it. When the first fleet arrived in Sydney Cove they sent convicts to Norfolk to work as farmers to produce food to send back to the colony. My ancestor, John Herbert was one such farmer. When the second fleet arrived more were sent there, mostly women. John Herbert married Hannah Bolton and they had 5 children on the island. They were able to build a house and were given some land for a home garden which Hannah worked during the week. John worked for the governor six days a week and after attending church on Sunday morning, he would work his own land during the afternoon. He was a hard worker and a valued worker and was made a policeman during his time there. Sadly, Hannah died on the island. The governor’ wife took a shine to John’s youngest child and after John agreed she took her back to England when they left after the settlement was closed  because the colony had become self sufficient. I have seen the place where John’s house had been and I found where Hannah had been buried although there were no grave stones there. The farmers were sent to places to settle in other colonies. Some were given grants of land in Tasmania in two places, New Norfolk in the south and  Norfolk plains in the north around the area of Longford. We also know where John’s land and home is, as I live in Tasmania. One of John’s daughters came to Tasmania and married a local gentleman. He worked the land with John and as John got older he moved out of the homestead into Westbury, a town close by, where he died and was buried. 
The second settlement on Norfolk Island was a penal settlement where convicts who were considered bad were sent. They were treated horribly and it was a dark stain on the history of the Island 
My husband and I visited the island for a week and had a wonderful time. There are plenty of places to visit and tours to go on. We stayed at a cabin and paid extra for a car while there. We found no problem with buying food from the supermarket. There were many shops and places to eat. We drove all around the island and spent several hours searching through the archives for information about John Herbert, which we could photocopy and bring home with us. The two things that we found interesting were giving way to the cows on the road and the early time the shops closed.
I encourage everyone to fly to the island and enjoy the diverse experiences as we did.
The second settlement on Norfolk Island was as a penal settlement

comments.author: @TravelHorizon-4K
comments.text: Was Australia’s abolition of Norfolk Island’s self-governance in 2015 a necessary reality check or an infringement on self-determination? On one hand, residents gained Medicare and welfare safety nets; on the other, they lost legislative independence and face mainland tax burdens. Is this 'modernization' slowly erasing Norfolk's unique cultural identity?

replies.author: @brianwatts5885
replies.text: Norfolk Islanders wanted Australia to fund them, but without legislative input.  Like "give us the money, but don't tell us what to do".  So from 2015 it was "we'll give you the money, but only if we get a say in what you do.  And, by the way, from now on you can pay tax".
